content.text: Breaking News More (-1) » Local News John Glenn Columbus permanently closing walking lot in preparation for terminal expansion The walking lot will close in early May for a new public safety building. Credit: WBNS-10TV File photo, John Glenn Columbus International Airport Author: 10TV Web Staff Published: 9:53 AM EDT April 15, 2026 Updated: 9:53 AM EDT April 15, 2026 COLUMBUS, Ohio — The walking lot at John Glenn Columbus International Airport will close in May to make room for a new building as part of the airport's terminal expansion. According to Columbus Regional Airport Authority, the lot will close permanently on May 4 to make room for a new public safety building. The building is part of CMH Next, the airport's new terminal project. The safety building will hold the public safety communications center and feature offices and training facilities. Airport authorities encourage travelers who often use the walking lot to use the valet service or other available parking options, including a parking garage or the red and green shuttle lots. RELATED: Final approvals made for new terminal at John Glenn Columbus International Airport "We know the Walking Lot has its loyal fans and understand this one might sting a bit. We’ll miss it too," airport representatives wrote in a Facebook post. "This change is part of the exciting progress happening across the airport — bringing us closer to a new terminal and opening day." The $2 billion terminal project will add a new, nearly 1-million-square-foot terminal. The project also features a new parking garage connected by a pedestrian bridge. According to airport representatives, the terminal is meant to "meet the demands" of the growing Columbus region. The new Columbus airport terminal is scheduled to open in early 2029. Volunteers from Google, in partnership with Columbus Recreation and Parks, gathered at Nafzger Park to plant trees and remove invasive species. About 20 volunteers were at the park, digging, planting and removing invasive species, like honeysuckle, from the park’s environment. Volunteer services manager, Betty Blockinger, with Columbus Recreation and Parks, said that removing invasive species helps the natural species survive. Blockinger said that anyone who didn’t make it to the event on Wednesday can still contribute to the conservation of the planet in several ways. "Pick up litter when they see it, they can always plant a tree in their yard — or pollinator garden," Blockinger said. "Anything you can do to help out the earth is a good thing." For more information about volunteering events, visit Columbus Recreation and Parks' website here.
